query: For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the onset or suppression of corrosion-related degradation in harsh environments at room and elevated temperatures? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to the untreated reference, applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: In uncoated, pre-exposed Q235 steel, the formation and integrity of a spontaneously generated iron oxide/hydroxide passivation film govern corrosion-related degradation. At room temperature, the gradual formation of a uniform passivation layer can slow corrosion onset, whereas at elevated temperatures the kinetics accelerate both film growth and its subsequent breakdown by chloride attack, resulting in pitting corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: Pre-exposed Q235 steel with its native microstructure and surface finish (no additional coatings or surface modifications).
generation.intervention: Exposure of the steel samples to a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution under controlled laboratory conditions at room temperature (≈25°C) and an elevated temperature (≈60–80°C).
generation.conditions: Harsh saline (chloride-rich) environment with controlled pH and constant chloride concentration under stagnant conditions, ensuring that any differences are due to temperature effects on the native passivation film formation and stability.
generation.structural_mediator: The integrity and continuity of the spontaneously formed iron oxide/hydroxide layer on the steel surface, acting as a passivation film.
generation.mechanism: Surface oxidation in the saline environment leads to the formation of a passivation layer (predominantly Fe2O3/FeOOH). At room temperature, slower reaction kinetics favor the development of a relatively uniform and protective film that retards further corrosion. At elevated temperatures, although film formation is initially faster, thermal stresses and increased chloride ion mobility lead to film instability and localized breakdown (pitting), thereby accelerating corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples held at room temperature will exhibit lower corrosion current density and fewer localized pitting incidents due to a more stable passive film, whereas samples at elevated temperatures will show significantly higher corrosion rates and pronounced pitting as a result of passivation film degradation.
generation.baseline: Q235 steel maintained in a non-corrosive, neutral environment where minimal formation or disruption of the passive film occurs, resulting in negligible corrosion.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies specifically to uncoated Q235 steel with its native surface conditions. Variations such as differences in surface roughness, ambient atmospheric exposure prior to testing, or changes in chloride concentration and pH could influence film formation kinetics and corrosion behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The exact composition and microstructural details of the native passivation film on Q235 steel, and how subtle variations in pre-exposure surface conditions affect film stability under different temperatures, remain to be thoroughly characterized.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of identical, pre-exposed Q235 steel samples with a standardized surface finish. Divide the samples into two groups: one exposed to 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution at room temperature (≈25°C) and the other at an elevated temperature (≈60–80°C). Monitor the corrosion behavior over time using electrochemical techniques and surface analyses.
measurements: Potentiodynamic polarization curves to determine corrosion current densities and pitting potentials.
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to evaluate the integrity of the passive film.
Surface characterization using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) to assess film composition and pitting morphology.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no significant differences are observed in corrosion current densities, pitting potentials, or passive film integrity between room temperature and elevated temperature samples, then the hypothesis that film instability at elevated temperatures escalates corrosion would be falsified.

## Abstract
In this paper, the (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 high-entropy alloy (HEA) coating with a thickness of 500 μm on Q235 steel substrate was fabricated by plasma spraying. The microscopic results showed that a new Laves phase is formed in the (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating compared to the HEA powder, and elemental segregation occurs between the dendrites and the interdendrites of the coating, while the interdendritic phase enriches with the Cr and Nb. The phase composition change and elemental segregation behavior were mainly due to the faster cooling rate of the plasma spraying technique. At the junction of the coating and the substrate, the HEA coating bonded well to the substrate; in addition, the width of transition zone was merely 2 μm. The microhardness of the (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating was 321 HV0.5, which is significantly higher than that of the substrate. In terms of corrosion resistance, the (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating has good corrosion resistance in NaCl solution. ## Abstract
AbstractIn this paper, CoCrFeNiTix high entropy alloy (HEA) coatings were prepared on the surface of Q235 steel by laser cladding. The microstructure, microhardness, and corrosion resistance of the coatings were studied. The mechanism of their corrosion resistance was elucidated experimentally and by first-principles calculations. The results show that CoCrFeNiTi0.1 adopts a face-centered cubic (FCC) phase, CoCrFeNiTi0.3 exhibits an FCC phase and a tetragonal FeCr phase, and CoCrFeNiTi0.5 adopts an FCC phase, a tetragonal FeCr phase, and a rhombohedral NiTi phase. The FCC phase, tetragonal FeCr phase, rhombohedral NiTi phase, and hexagonal CoTi phase are all observed in the CoCrFeNiTi0.7 HEA. The alloys assume the dendritic structure that is typical of HEAs. Ni and Ti are enriched in the interdendritic regions, whereas Cr and Fe are enriched in the dendrites. With increasing Ti content, the hardness of the cladding layers also increases due to the combined effects of lattice distortion and dispersion strengthening.
